title: Week 2: dplyr and Census
text:
RStudio, Scripts, and Code Chunks
There are several ways to write and run R code.

The Console
The R Console runs code immediately and displays the result:
2 + 2
The Console is useful for quick experiments. However, code entered there is temporary in the sense that it is not automatically saved as part of a reproducible analysis. The objects remain in the current R session, but they can disappear when the session is restarted.


R Scripts
An R script contains R code saved in a file with the .R extension:
result <- 2 + 2
Scripts are useful for saving and rerunning code.


Quarto Code Chunks
A Quarto document can contain written explanations and executable R code:

2 + 2

[1] 4


When the document is rendered, the code runs and its result appears in the final webpage.
A useful mental model is:

The Console is for experimentation.
An R script is for saving code.
A Quarto document is for combining code, explanation, and results.

title: Week 2: dplyr and Census
text:
Packages
An R package is a collection of functions and data that extends what R can do.
You usually install a package once:
install.packages("dplyr")
Installing a package is like buying a book. You normally do not need to buy the same book every time you want to read it.
Before using a package in a new R session, load it:
library(dplyr)
Loading a package is like taking the book off the shelf so that you can use it.
For example:
library(tidycensus)
You generally load the package each time you start a new R session and want to use it.
The correct spelling is:
library(dplyr)
not:
library(deplyr)

title: Week 2: dplyr and Census
text:
Tibbles and Data Frames
A tibble is a modern version of an R data frame. Both store data in rows and columns, but tibbles print more clearly and provide more information when displayed.
For example:
county_data
A tibble usually shows:

The column names
The data types
A limited number of rows
The number of observations and variables

A tibble is not a verb. It is a type of data object.

title: Week 2: dplyr and Census
text:
R Is Case-Sensitive
R treats uppercase and lowercase letters as different.
These are different names:
select()
Select()
The correct tidyverse function is:
select()
This also applies to object and column names:
moe_pct
MOE_PCT
These are not the same column name.

title: Week 2: dplyr and Census
text:
Common Data-Verbs
The tidyverse provides functions that work like verbs. Each function performs a common data operation.

filter() Selects Rows
filter() keeps rows that meet a condition.
large_counties <- filter(
  counties,
  population > 5000
)
This keeps counties whose population is greater than 5,000.
A helpful way to remember it is:

filter() chooses observations.



select() Selects Columns
select() keeps particular columns.
county_subset <- select(
  counties,
  NAME,
  population
)
This keeps only the NAME and population columns.
A helpful way to remember it is:

select() chooses variables.



mutate() Creates or Modifies Columns
mutate() creates a new column or changes an existing column.
new_counties <- mutate(
  counties,
  income_thousands = income / 1000
)
This creates a new column called income_thousands.
The general pattern is:
new_data <- mutate(
  old_data,
  new_column = calculation
)


arrange() Changes Row Order
arrange() sorts rows.
arrange(counties, population)
This sorts from smallest to largest population.
To sort from largest to smallest, use desc():
arrange(counties, desc(population))
The function is lowercase:
arrange()
not:
Arrange()


group_by() Defines Groups
group_by() tells R to treat observations as belonging to groups.
counties %>%
  group_by(state)
This does not summarize the data by itself. It prepares the data for a grouped operation.


summarize() Reduces Groups
summarize() calculates summary values for each group.
Suppose the data looks like this:



County
State
Income




Orange
NY
70,000


Nassau
NY
80,000


Sacramento
CA
100,000


Orange
NY
90,000



We can calculate the minimum income for each state:
counties %>%
  group_by(state) %>%
  summarize(
    min_income = min(income)
  )
The result would be:



State
Minimum income




NY
70,000


CA
100,000



group_by() defines the groups, while summarize() calculates the result for each group.

title: Week 2: dplyr and Census
text:
Pipes
Without pipes, a multi-step workflow may require several intermediate objects:
step1 <- filter(counties, moe_pct > 10)

step2 <- arrange(step1, desc(moe_pct))

step3 <- select(step2, NAME, moe_pct)
Pipes allow these steps to be connected:
new_data <- counties %>%
  filter(moe_pct > 10) %>%
  arrange(desc(moe_pct)) %>%
  select(NAME, moe_pct)
The pipe passes the result from one function into the next.
In plain language, this means:

Start with counties.
Keep counties where moe_pct is greater than 10.
Sort them from largest to smallest moe_pct.
Keep only NAME and moe_pct.

R also has a newer native pipe:
new_data <- counties |>
  filter(moe_pct > 10) |>
  arrange(desc(moe_pct)) |>
  select(NAME, moe_pct)
Both %>% and |> are used to build readable workflows.

title: Week 2: dplyr and Census
section: The U.S. Census and the ACS
text:
The U.S. Census and the ACS
The U.S. Constitution requires a population count every ten years. This is called the Decennial Census.
The Decennial Census counts people living in the United States, regardless of citizenship or immigration status. Its main purpose is to produce a complete population count and support political representation and resource allocation.
The American Community Survey, or ACS, is different. It is an ongoing sample survey that collects information about topics such as:

Income
Education
Employment
Housing
Disability
Race and ethnicity
Transportation
Health-related characteristics

The ACS uses a sample of households to estimate characteristics for the wider population.

title: Week 2: dplyr and Census
text:
ACS Products

ACS 1-Year Estimates
ACS 1-year estimates are generally available for larger populations and places. They provide more recent estimates but may not be available for smaller areas.


ACS 3-Year Estimates
The ACS 3-year estimates were discontinued after the 2013 data release.


ACS 5-Year Estimates
ACS 5-year estimates combine five years of survey data. They are available for smaller populations and smaller geographies, including census tracts and, for many variables, block groups.
For example, a 2023 ACS 5-year estimate generally represents data collected during:
2019–2023
It is not a single-year estimate. It summarizes information collected across the five-year period.

title: Week 2: dplyr and Census
text:
Estimates and Margins of Error
ACS results include an estimate and a margin of error.
For example:
Estimate = 38.7
Margin of error = 0.2
This can be written as:
38.7 ± 0.2
The estimate is the reported value, while the margin of error describes the uncertainty around that estimate.
Smaller places often have smaller samples. Because fewer households are surveyed, estimates for small places can have larger margins of error.

title: Week 2: dplyr and Census
text:
Census Variable Codes
Census variables have codes that identify the table, line, and type of value.
For example:
B19013_001E
The code can be understood as:

B = base table
19013 = table number
001 = line number
E = estimate

The margin-of-error version uses M:
B19013_001M
In many tidycensus functions, the estimate variable can be requested without the final E:
"B19013_001"
However, the full Census variable code is often shown as:
B19013_001E

title: Week 2: dplyr and Census
text:
Finding Census Variables
The load_variables() function retrieves the Census variable dictionary.
library(tidycensus)

variables <- load_variables(
  year = 2023,
  dataset = "acs5"
)
This gives information about available variables, including:

Variable codes
Variable labels
Table names
Concepts

load_variables() helps identify and understand variables. It does not download the actual county data.

title: Week 2: dplyr and Census
text:
Downloading ACS Data
The get_acs() function downloads ACS data.
library(tidycensus)

data <- get_acs(
  geography = "county",
  variables = c(
    "B19013_001",
    "B01003_001"
  ),
  state = "PA",
  year = 2023,
  survey = "acs5"
)
This requests two variables for Pennsylvania counties using the 2023 ACS 5-year survey.
The result is usually returned in tidy, long format.

title: Week 2: dplyr and Census
text:
Census Geographies
A census tract is a statistical area designed to represent a relatively small community. A tract usually contains approximately 1,200 to 8,000 people, with an ideal population of about 4,000.
A tract can be used as a rough geographic proxy for a neighborhood, although a tract is not always the same as a socially recognized neighborhood.
Census tracts are generally revised during the decennial Census. Their boundaries can change, which makes comparisons across years more difficult.
To compare geography consistently over time, researchers sometimes use harmonized geography products such as:

NHGIS
LTDB

These products provide tools or crosswalks for comparing geographic areas across different boundary systems.
Block groups are smaller than census tracts. Because they contain fewer people, their estimates can have larger margins of error.
A census block is the smallest Census geography. Blocks are used in the Decennial Census but generally do not have the same level of ACS data available as larger geographies.

title: Week 2: dplyr and Census
text:
GEOIDs
A GEOID is a unique identifier for a Census geography.
A county GEOID contains five digits:
Two-digit state code + three-digit county code
A census tract GEOID contains eleven digits:
Two-digit state code
+ three-digit county code
+ six-digit tract code
A block-group GEOID contains twelve digits:
Census tract GEOID + one-digit block-group code
GEOIDs should usually be stored as character strings rather than numbers.
For example:
06001
If this value is stored as a number, R may remove the leading zero:
6001
That can cause problems when joining Census data to geographic boundary data.

title: Week 2: dplyr and Census
text:
Long and Wide Data
By default, get_acs() returns data in long format.
In long format, each geography-variable combination usually occupies its own row. This is useful when working with one variable at a time or creating maps.
Wide format places multiple variables in separate columns. This is often more convenient when comparing variables or calculating relationships between them.
To request wide data directly:
county_wide <- get_acs(
  geography = "county",
  variables = c(
    myvar = "B01002_001",
    pop = "B01003_001"
  ),
  state = "CA",
  year = 2023,
  survey = "acs5",
  output = "wide"
)
Because the variables were named myvar and pop, the resulting columns will include:
myvarE
myvarM
popE
popM
The suffixes mean:

E = estimate
M = margin of error

For example:
county_wide <- county_wide %>%
  mutate(
    moe_pct = myvarM / myvarE * 100
  )
This calculates the margin of error as a percentage of the estimate.

title: Week 2: dplyr and Census
text:
A Complete Data Workflow
A typical workflow might look like this:
library(tidyverse)
library(tidycensus)

county_data <- get_acs(
  geography = "county",
  variables = "B01002_001",
  state = "CA",
  year = 2023,
  survey = "acs5"
)

county_data <- county_data %>%
  mutate(
    moe_pct = moe / estimate * 100
  ) %>%
  arrange(desc(moe_pct)) %>%
  select(NAME, estimate, moe, moe_pct)

head(county_data, 10)
This workflow:

Downloads county-level ACS data.
Calculates the relative margin of error.
Sorts counties from highest to lowest relative margin of error.
Keeps only the relevant columns.
Displays the ten counties with the largest relative margins of error.

title: Week 2: dplyr and Census
text:
Key Lessons
This week, I learned that R analysis is often built as a sequence of small transformations. Each function performs one task, and pipes allow those tasks to be connected into a readable workflow.
I also learned that Census data requires attention to geography, time period, variable definitions, estimates, and margins of error. A reported estimate should not automatically be treated as equally reliable across all places. Smaller geographies often have smaller samples and greater uncertainty.

title: Week 2: dplyr and Census
text:
Common Mistakes to Avoid

Use library(dplyr), not library(deplyr).
R functions are case-sensitive, so use select() and arrange().
Close every pipe and parenthesis correctly.
Make sure column names match exactly.
Store GEOIDs as character strings.
Remember that ACS 5-year estimates cover five years of data.
Do not confuse an estimate with its margin of error.
Use load_variables() to understand variables and get_acs() to download data.
Use output = "wide" when comparing multiple variables side by side.

title: About Me
text:
I am a Ghanaian geospatial scientist and GIS team lead with a background in Geospatial Engineering. Before joining Penn’s Master of Urban Spatial Analytics program, I worked at Zipline International in Kigali, where I helped develop geospatial systems for autonomous medical drone delivery. This work involved terrain modeling, aerial imagery, route planning, and spatial data management across complex environments. It showed me how geospatial technology can have a direct human impact, from helping patients receive medical supplies on time to improving access to essential services.
My interest in urban spatial analytics grew from seeing how invisible or incomplete spatial data can limit effective planning. Earlier in my career, I worked on mapping underserved communities and sanitation infrastructure, producing information that helped support improved sanitation for more than 3,000 communities. These experiences taught me that maps are not just technical products. They influence how resources are allocated, which communities receive attention, and how governments and organizations respond to urgent needs.
At MUSA, I am strengthening my skills in statistics, programming, spatial modeling, data visualization, and urban systems. I am particularly interested in routing, mapping, geospatial software, and the spatial intelligence that supports technologies such as delivery platforms, autonomous vehicles, and self-driving systems. I hope to work with technology companies developing products that depend on accurate maps, efficient routing, and a strong understanding of the built environment.
Across these interests, my central goal is to help create a more equitable society. Whether I am working on public infrastructure, medical delivery, transportation, or autonomous technology, I want to contribute to systems that are more accessible, reliable, and responsive to the needs of underserved communities.

title: Assignment 2: Who Do We Know the Least About?
text:
The question
Every number the American Community Survey publishes is an estimate drawn from a sample, not a count. That means every number comes with a margin of error — a statement about how wrong it might be.
Most people ignore it. In this assignment, you won’t.






TipDelete this box



Rewrite the paragraph below in your own words once you’ve picked your state and variable. Two or three sentences saying what you’re looking at and why.


In this analysis, I look at [YOUR VARIABLE] across counties in [YOUR STATE], and ask which communities we measure most and least reliably.

title: Assignment 2: Who Do We Know the Least About?
section: How big is the margin of error?
text:
How big is the margin of error?
A margin of error of 3,000 means something very different for an estimate of 20,000 than for an estimate of 200,000. To compare across places, we need it as a percentage.

county_data <- county_data %>%
  mutate(moe_pct = moe / estimate * 100)


county_data %>%
  arrange(desc(moe_pct)) %>%
  select(NAME, estimate, moe, moe_pct) %>%
  head(10)

# A tibble: 10 × 4
   NAME                         estimate   moe moe_pct
   <chr>                           <dbl> <dbl>   <dbl>
 1 Alpine County, California        41.1   4.8   11.7 
 2 Sierra County, California        56     5      8.93
 3 Mono County, California          40.3   1.8    4.47
 4 Modoc County, California         49     2.1    4.29
 5 Colusa County, California        35.7   0.9    2.52
 6 Del Norte County, California     40.8   0.9    2.21
 7 Mariposa County, California      51.6   1      1.94
 8 Trinity County, California       54.8   0.9    1.64
 9 Lassen County, California        37.8   0.6    1.59
10 Plumas County, California        52.1   0.8    1.54



Alpine County is the least reliable county in the dataset, with the highest relative margin of error(moe_pct) at approximately 11.68%.

title: Assignment 2: Who Do We Know the Least About?
text:
Sorting counties into reliability categories

county_data <- county_data %>%
  mutate(reliability = case_when(
    moe_pct < 1  ~ "High confidence",
    moe_pct < 4  ~ "Moderate",
    TRUE         ~ "Low confidence"
  ))

count(county_data, reliability)

# A tibble: 3 × 2
  reliability         n
  <chr>           <int>
1 High confidence    42
2 Low confidence      4
3 Moderate           12


Using the original thresholds, 56 counties were classified as high confidence, 1 as moderate, and 1 as low confidence. Because this classification was highly concentrated in one category, I adjusted the thresholds to 1% and 4% to make differences in relative margin of error more informative for this county-level dataset.

title: Assignment 2: Who Do We Know the Least About?
section: Is the margin of error bigger in small places?
text:
Is the margin of error bigger in small places?
To answer this we need population and our variable side by side, in the same row. That means a wide pull.

county_wide <- get_acs(
  geography = "county",
  variables = c(myvar = my_variable,
                pop   = "B01003_001"),
  state = my_state,
  year = 2023,
  survey = "acs5",
  output = "wide"
)

head(county_wide)

# A tibble: 6 × 6
  GEOID NAME                         myvarE myvarM    popE  popM
  <chr> <chr>                         <dbl>  <dbl>   <dbl> <dbl>
1 06001 Alameda County, California     38.7    0.2 1651949    NA
2 06003 Alpine County, California      41.1    4.8    1695   234
3 06005 Amador County, California      49.9    0.6   41029    NA
4 06007 Butte County, California       36.3    0.2  209470    NA
5 06009 Calaveras County, California   52      0.7   45995    NA
6 06011 Colusa County, California      35.7    0.9   21895    NA



county_wide <- county_wide %>%
  mutate(moe_pct = myvarM / myvarE * 100) %>%
  mutate(reliability = case_when(
    moe_pct < 5  ~ "High confidence",
    moe_pct < 15 ~ "Moderate",
    TRUE         ~ "Low confidence"
  ))

Now compare the average population of counties in each reliability category.

county_wide %>%
  group_by(reliability) %>%
  summarize(
    n_counties = n(),
    avg_population = mean(popE)
  )

# A tibble: 2 × 3
  reliability     n_counties avg_population
  <chr>                <int>          <dbl>
1 High confidence         56        700685.
2 Moderate                 2          2213

title: Assignment 2: Who Do We Know the Least About?
section: Optional challenges - For those craving more
text:
Optional challenges - For those craving more






NoteDelete this box



None of these are graded. There are no extra points. A complete, well-written assignment earns a 2 either way.
They’re here for anyone who finished the above and found it straightforward. Pick one (or more) that interests you.

Propagate the margin of error. If you compute a derived value — a percentage, a ratio, a sum — its uncertainty depends on the uncertainty of its inputs, and you can’t just carry the original MOE along. The Census Bureau publishes formulas for this, and tidycensus implements them: moe_sum(), moe_prop(), moe_ratio(). Compute something derived, and get its margin of error right.
Parameterize the report. Add params: to the YAML so the state is an input rather than hard-coded, and the same file regenerates for any state. Render it from the terminal with quarto render assignment2.qmd -P state:NY.
Write a function and iterate. Wrap the data pull in a function, then use purrr::map_dfr() to run it across several states at once. Does the small-places-are-noisier pattern hold everywhere, or are some states different?
Change the geographic scale. Run the same variable at geography = "tract" inside one county. Compare the margins of error to what you saw at county level. What does that imply about the resolution at which you can actually trust ACS data?

If you try one, add a short section describing what you did and what you found.

title: Week 1: Getting Set Up
text:
What Is a Website?
A website is a collection of files that a browser can display. These files usually include:

HTML, which provides the structure
CSS, which controls the appearance
JavaScript, which adds interactivity
Images and other supporting files

My portfolio is made from written source files and then converted into HTML pages by Quarto. GitHub Pages hosts those HTML files so that other people can view them online.
A simple mental model is:

Quarto creates the website, and GitHub Pages publishes it.

title: Week 1: Getting Set Up
text:
What Is Quarto?
Quarto is a publishing system that converts files written in .qmd format into HTML documents and other outputs such as PDFs, reports, presentations, books, and websites.
A .qmd file combines three things:

YAML, which contains document settings
Markdown, which contains my written content
Code chunks, which run code and display the results

Quarto is useful because it allows writing, coding, analysis, and presentation to exist in the same document.

title: Week 1: Getting Set Up
text:
How Quarto Works
When I click Render, Quarto processes the .qmd file from top to bottom.
Behind the scenes, it:

Reads the document settings in the YAML section.
Interprets the Markdown text.
Finds the code chunks.
Sends R code to R for evaluation.
Receives the results from R.
Combines my writing, code, and results.
Produces an HTML file.

The result is a finished webpage that can be viewed in a browser.

title: Week 1: Getting Set Up
text:
Anatomy of a .qmd File
A Quarto document usually looks like this:
---
title: "Week 1 Notes"
date: 2026-08-28+
---
This first section is called YAML. It contains metadata and settings for the document.
The body of the document contains Markdown:
## What I Learned

Quarto lets me combine written explanations with executable R code.

[Visit my portfolio](index.qmd)
The document can also contain an R code chunk:

2 + 2

[1] 4


When the document is rendered, the result of the calculation appears underneath the code.

title: Week 1: Getting Set Up
text:
Files and Folders
Different files in the project serve different purposes.

Files for the website

index.qmd is the homepage.
about.qmd is the About page.
weekly-notes/ contains my weekly notes.
assignments/ contains my assignments.



Files for the tools

_quarto.yml contains settings for the entire Quarto website.
freeze/ stores rendered results so that some code does not need to run again.
.Rproj identifies the project as an RStudio project.
.gitignore tells Git which files it should ignore.
.Renviron stores environment variables and private information such as API keys.
docs/ contains the HTML files generated by Quarto for publication.

The files I write are the source files. The files in docs/ are the rendered website.

title: Week 1: Getting Set Up
text:
How Pages Become Website URLs
The homepage file is usually named index.qmd. When Quarto renders the website, it creates:
docs/index.html
GitHub Pages then displays that file at the main website address.
The same pattern applies to folders:
weekly-notes/index.qmd
        ↓
docs/weekly-notes/index.html
        ↓
myname.github.io/weekly-notes/
The index file acts as the default page for its folder.

title: Week 1: Getting Set Up
text:
Git, GitHub, and GitHub Desktop
These three tools are related, but they are not the same thing.

Git
Git is a version-control system that runs on my computer. It records changes to files and allows me to save labelled snapshots of my work.


GitHub.com
GitHub.com is an online service that stores a copy of my project repository. It also makes the project accessible for collaboration and publishing.


GitHub Desktop
GitHub Desktop is a graphical interface for Git. It provides buttons for common Git actions.
Two important Git actions are:

Commit: Save a labelled snapshot of changes on my computer.
Push: Send those committed changes to GitHub.com.

After I push changes, GitHub Pages can update the live version of my portfolio.

title: Week 1: Getting Set Up
text:
R Scripts and Quarto Documents
An R script contains mainly R code:
x <- 10
x + 5
A Quarto document is more flexible. It can contain:

Written explanations
Headings
Links
Images
R code
Tables
Charts
Code results

This makes Quarto useful for documenting not only what I calculated, but also why I calculated it and what the results mean.

title: Week 1: Getting Set Up
text:
My Mental Model
I now think of my portfolio as having three versions:

My computer: where I edit the source files
GitHub.com: where Git stores and tracks the project
My live website: what visitors see in their browser

The complete process is:
Write or edit a .qmd file
        ↓
Render it with Quarto
        ↓
Review the generated HTML
        ↓
Commit the changes with Git
        ↓
Push the commit to GitHub
        ↓
GitHub Pages updates the website

title: Week 1: Getting Set Up
text:
Reflection
This week helped me understand that my portfolio is not created directly in the browser. I write source files in Quarto, render them into HTML, and then use GitHub Pages to publish the result. The most important idea for me was separating the source files from the finished website. I am still building confidence with the workflow, but I now have a clearer understanding of how R, Quarto, Git, GitHub, and GitHub Pages work together.

title: Assignment 2: Who Do We Know the Least About?
text:
The question
Every number the American Community Survey publishes is an estimate drawn from a sample, not a count. That means every number comes with a margin of error — a statement about how wrong it might be.
Most people ignore it. In this assignment, you won’t.

title: Assignment 2: Who Do We Know the Least About?
text:
Choosing what to measure

my_state <- "CA"        # two-letter abbreviation, in quotes
my_variable <- "B01002_001"     # the variable code, in quotes

title: Assignment 2: Who Do We Know the Least About?
text:
Pulling the data

county_data <- get_acs(
  geography = "county",
  variables = my_variable,
  state = my_state,
  year = 2023,
  survey = "acs5"
)

Let’s look at what came back.

dim(county_data)

[1] 58  5

head(county_data)

# A tibble: 6 × 5
  GEOID NAME                         variable   estimate   moe
  <chr> <chr>                        <chr>         <dbl> <dbl>
1 06001 Alameda County, California   B01002_001     38.7   0.2
2 06003 Alpine County, California    B01002_001     41.1   4.8
3 06005 Amador County, California    B01002_001     49.9   0.6
4 06007 Butte County, California     B01002_001     36.3   0.2
5 06009 Calaveras County, California B01002_001     52     0.7
6 06011 Colusa County, California    B01002_001     35.7   0.9


California has 58 counties and that number matches the number of rows (58) returned by checking the dimensions of the data.

title: Assignment 2: Who Do We Know the Least About?
section: How big is the margin of error?
text:
How big is the margin of error?
A margin of error of 3,000 means something very different for an estimate of 20,000 than for an estimate of 200,000. To compare across places, we need it as a percentage.

county_data <- county_data %>%
  mutate(moe_pct = moe / estimate * 100)


county_data %>%
  arrange(desc(moe_pct)) %>%
  select(NAME, estimate, moe, moe_pct) %>%
  head(10)

# A tibble: 10 × 4
   NAME                         estimate   moe moe_pct
   <chr>                           <dbl> <dbl>   <dbl>
 1 Alpine County, California        41.1   4.8   11.7 
 2 Sierra County, California        56     5      8.93
 3 Mono County, California          40.3   1.8    4.47
 4 Modoc County, California         49     2.1    4.29
 5 Colusa County, California        35.7   0.9    2.52
 6 Del Norte County, California     40.8   0.9    2.21
 7 Mariposa County, California      51.6   1      1.94
 8 Trinity County, California       54.8   0.9    1.64
 9 Lassen County, California        37.8   0.6    1.59
10 Plumas County, California        52.1   0.8    1.54


Alpine County is the least reliable county in the dataset, with the highest relative margin of error(moe_pct) at approximately 11.68%.

title: Assignment 2: Who Do We Know the Least About?
text:
Sorting counties into reliability categories

county_data <- county_data %>%
  mutate(reliability = case_when(
    moe_pct < 1  ~ "High confidence",
    moe_pct < 4  ~ "Moderate",
    TRUE         ~ "Low confidence"
  ))

count(county_data, reliability)

# A tibble: 3 × 2
  reliability         n
  <chr>           <int>
1 High confidence    42
2 Low confidence      4
3 Moderate           12


Using the original thresholds, 56 counties were classified as high confidence, 1 as moderate, and 1 as low confidence. Because this classification was highly concentrated in one category, I adjusted the thresholds to 1% and 4% to make differences in relative margin of error more informative for this county-level dataset.

title: Assignment 2: Who Do We Know the Least About?
section: Is the margin of error bigger in small places?
text:
Is the margin of error bigger in small places?
To answer this we need population and our variable side by side, in the same row. That means a wide pull.

county_wide <- get_acs(
  geography = "county",
  variables = c(myvar = my_variable,
                pop   = "B01003_001"),
  state = my_state,
  year = 2023,
  survey = "acs5",
  output = "wide"
)

head(county_wide)

# A tibble: 6 × 6
  GEOID NAME                         myvarE myvarM    popE  popM
  <chr> <chr>                         <dbl>  <dbl>   <dbl> <dbl>
1 06001 Alameda County, California     38.7    0.2 1651949    NA
2 06003 Alpine County, California      41.1    4.8    1695   234
3 06005 Amador County, California      49.9    0.6   41029    NA
4 06007 Butte County, California       36.3    0.2  209470    NA
5 06009 Calaveras County, California   52      0.7   45995    NA
6 06011 Colusa County, California      35.7    0.9   21895    NA



county_wide <- county_wide %>%
  mutate(moe_pct = myvarM / myvarE * 100) %>%
  mutate(reliability = case_when(
    moe_pct < 1  ~ "High confidence",
    moe_pct < 4 ~ "Moderate",
    TRUE         ~ "Low confidence"
  ))

Now compare the average population of counties in each reliability category.

county_wide %>%
  group_by(reliability) %>%
  summarize(
    n_counties = n(),
    avg_population = mean(popE)
  )

# A tibble: 3 × 3
  reliability     n_counties avg_population
  <chr>                <int>          <dbl>
1 High confidence         42        924758.
2 Low confidence           4          6560.
3 Moderate                12         31394.


The high-confidence counties had an average population of 924,758, compared with 31,394 for the moderate-confidence counties and only 6,560.25 for low-confidence counties. The pattern suggests that smaller counties tend to have larger relative margins of error and less reliable estimates.

title: Assignment 2: Who Do We Know the Least About?
text:
What this means for policy
The least reliable estimates came from Alpine, Sierra, Mono, and Modoc Counties. Their average population was 6,560, compared with 924,758 for the 42 high-confidence counties.
This happens because the ACS uses a sample of households. Smaller counties have fewer households in the sample, so their estimates have more uncertainty and larger margins of error.
If a state agency treated every estimate as equally reliable, these rural counties could receive less funding than they need for healthcare, transportation, housing, or services for older residents. Funding decisions should account for both the estimate and its margin of error.

title: Assignment 2: Who Do We Know the Least About?
text:
My Reflections
This week helped me understand how R can be used to move from raw data to a clear result. I practiced using tidyverse functions such as filter(), select(), mutate(), arrange(), group_by(), and summarize(). Using pipes also made the code easier to follow because I could connect several steps without creating a new object after every operation.
I also learned how to use tidycensus to download American Community Survey data. Before this, I mostly thought of Census data as a table of numbers. Working with estimates and margins of error showed me that the numbers also have different levels of reliability. In my county analysis, the smaller counties had much larger relative margins of error than the larger counties. The four low-confidence counties had an average population of 6,560, while the 42 high-confidence counties had an average population of 924,758.
The exercise also showed me why it is important to understand the structure of the data before analyzing it. I had to distinguish between long and wide formats, identify the estimate and margin-of-error columns, and make sure my reliability cutoffs were applied consistently. I am still getting used to R syntax, but the workflow is becoming clearer. The optional, non-scoring problems will require more practice because I need to build a stronger understanding of the concepts before I can work through them independently.
